title: Chemical Laboratory Technology
source_note: Grounded in standard NUC-aligned chemical laboratory technology curricula: glassware and apparatus, volumetric analysis, qualitative/gravimetric analysis, solution preparation and calculations, and chemical lab safety typical of a 200-level Science Laboratory Technology programme.

questions.question: Which piece of glassware is most accurate for delivering a fixed, precise volume of liquid such as 25.00 mL in a titration?
options: A volumetric (bulb) pipette
A measuring cylinder
A beaker
A conical flask
questions.correct_answer: A volumetric (bulb) pipette
questions.explanation: A volumetric pipette is calibrated to deliver one specific, highly precise volume, unlike a measuring cylinder which has lower precision.

questions.question: What is the function of a burette in a titration experiment?
options: To deliver a variable, precisely measurable volume of titrant into the analyte
To store large volumes of stock solution
To weigh solid reagents accurately
To heat solutions to boiling
questions.correct_answer: To deliver a variable, precisely measurable volume of titrant into the analyte
questions.explanation: A burette has a graduated scale and stopcock that allow controlled, incremental addition of titrant, with the volume delivered read from the scale.

questions.question: In reading the meniscus of a burette or volumetric flask containing a clear aqueous solution, the reading should be taken at:
options: The bottom of the concave meniscus, at eye level
The top of the meniscus, viewed from above
Either the top or bottom, it does not matter
The point where the liquid touches the glass wall
questions.correct_answer: The bottom of the concave meniscus, at eye level
questions.explanation: For most aqueous solutions, the meniscus curves downward (concave); the reading is taken at the lowest point at eye level to avoid parallax error.

questions.question: Before use, a burette should be rinsed with:
options: A small portion of the solution it will contain
Only distilled water, then used immediately while still wet
Concentrated acid regardless of the titrant
Soap solution left in the burette
questions.correct_answer: A small portion of the solution it will contain
questions.explanation: Rinsing with the solution to be used prevents dilution of the titrant by residual water left from washing, ensuring accurate concentration during titration.

questions.question: In an acid-base titration, phenolphthalein indicator changes from colourless to pink at approximately which pH range?
questions.explanation: Phenolphthalein is colourless in acidic/neutral solution and turns pink in basic solution, transitioning over approximately pH 8.2 to 10.0.

questions.question: Methyl orange indicator is most suitable for titrating:
options: A strong acid against a weak base
A weak acid against a strong base only
A weak acid against a weak base
Any titration regardless of strength
questions.correct_answer: A strong acid against a weak base
questions.explanation: Methyl orange changes colour in the acidic range (pH about 3.1-4.4), matching the equivalence point pH of a strong acid-weak base titration, which is acidic.

questions.question: 25.0 mL of HCl solution is exactly neutralized by 20.0 mL of 0.10 M NaOH. What is the concentration of the HCl?
questions.explanation: For a 1:1 reaction, moles NaOH = 0.020 L x 0.10 M = 0.0020 mol = moles HCl. Concentration HCl = 0.0020 mol / 0.025 L = 0.08 M.

questions.question: How would you prepare 250 mL of a 0.5 M NaOH solution from solid NaOH (molar mass 40 g/mol)?
options: Dissolve 5.0 g of NaOH in distilled water and make up to 250 mL in a volumetric flask
Dissolve 20.0 g of NaOH in 250 mL of water
Dissolve 0.5 g of NaOH in 250 mL of water
Dissolve 12.5 g of NaOH and make up to 500 mL
questions.correct_answer: Dissolve 5.0 g of NaOH in distilled water and make up to 250 mL in a volumetric flask
questions.explanation: Moles needed = 0.5 M x 0.250 L = 0.125 mol; mass = 0.125 mol x 40 g/mol = 5.0 g, dissolved and diluted to exactly 250 mL.

questions.question: What is the correct technique for making up a solution to the exact mark in a volumetric flask?
options: Add solvent until the bottom of the meniscus sits exactly on the calibration mark, viewed at eye level
Fill until liquid overflows slightly, then wipe the top
Add solvent until the flask feels full by weight
Estimate the mark by holding the flask up to the light only once
questions.correct_answer: Add solvent until the bottom of the meniscus sits exactly on the calibration mark, viewed at eye level
questions.explanation: Accurate volumetric preparation requires the meniscus bottom to align precisely with the graduation mark, read at eye level to avoid parallax.

questions.question: In gravimetric analysis, the final mass of a precipitate is determined only after it has been:
options: Filtered, washed, dried (or ignited) to constant mass, and cooled in a desiccator
Dissolved back into solution
Weighed while still wet
Left exposed to open air overnight without drying
questions.correct_answer: Filtered, washed, dried (or ignited) to constant mass, and cooled in a desiccator
questions.explanation: Gravimetric analysis requires removing all moisture and impurities and cooling in a desiccator to prevent reabsorption of atmospheric moisture before an accurate final weighing.

questions.question: Why is a precipitate washed with a dilute solution of an electrolyte (rather than pure water) in some gravimetric procedures?
options: To prevent peptization (the precipitate breaking up into a colloidal suspension that passes through the filter)
To increase the mass of the precipitate artificially
To dissolve the precipitate completely
Because pure water reacts explosively with all precipitates
questions.correct_answer: To prevent peptization (the precipitate breaking up into a colloidal suspension that passes through the filter)
questions.explanation: Some precipitates peptize (disperse into colloidal particles) when washed with pure water; a dilute electrolyte solution maintains ionic strength and prevents this loss.

questions.question: A white precipitate that dissolves in excess ammonia solution to form a soluble complex, and forms a curdy white precipitate with silver nitrate, most likely indicates the presence of which anion?
options: Chloride (Cl-)
Sulphate (SO4^2-)
Nitrate (NO3-)
Carbonate (CO3^2-)
questions.correct_answer: Chloride (Cl-)
questions.explanation: Chloride ions form a curdy white AgCl precipitate with silver nitrate that is soluble in excess dilute ammonia, a classic qualitative test for chloride.

questions.question: In qualitative inorganic analysis, addition of dilute HCl to a solid sample produces brisk effervescence with a colourless, odourless gas that turns limewater milky. This confirms the presence of:
options: Carbonate (CO3^2-)
Sulphide (S^2-)
Sulphite (SO3^2-)
Nitrite (NO2-)
questions.correct_answer: Carbonate (CO3^2-)
questions.explanation: Carbonates react with dilute acid to release CO2 gas, which is colourless, odourless, and turns limewater milky due to formation of insoluble calcium carbonate.

questions.question: A flame test on a solid sample produces a lilac (light purple) flame colour. This indicates the likely presence of which cation?
options: Potassium (K+)
Sodium (Na+)
Calcium (Ca2+)
Copper (Cu2+)
questions.correct_answer: Potassium (K+)
questions.explanation: Potassium salts characteristically produce a lilac flame colour in a flame test, distinguishing it from sodium (yellow) or calcium (brick-red).

questions.question: Which laboratory technique separates the components of a mixture based on differences in boiling point?
options: Distillation
Filtration
Decantation
Crystallization
questions.correct_answer: Distillation
questions.explanation: Distillation works by heating a liquid mixture and condensing the vapours; components with different boiling points vaporize and separate at different temperatures.

questions.question: Filtration is used in the laboratory primarily to separate:
options: An insoluble solid from a liquid
Two miscible liquids
Dissolved salts from their solvent by evaporation
Gases from one another
questions.correct_answer: An insoluble solid from a liquid
questions.explanation: Filtration uses a porous medium (filter paper) to retain insoluble solid particles while allowing the liquid (filtrate) to pass through.

questions.question: Recrystallization is used to purify a solid compound based on the principle that:
options: The solubility of the compound in a solvent increases with temperature, allowing pure crystals to form on cooling
All impurities are always insoluble in any solvent
Heating a solid always destroys impurities chemically
The compound must first be converted into a gas
questions.correct_answer: The solubility of the compound in a solvent increases with temperature, allowing pure crystals to form on cooling
questions.explanation: Recrystallization dissolves the impure solid in hot solvent, then slowly cools it so pure crystals grow, leaving soluble impurities in the mother liquor.

questions.question: In liquid-liquid extraction using a separating funnel, the two layers that form are separated based on:
options: Difference in density between the two immiscible liquids
Difference in colour only
Difference in boiling point
Difference in electrical conductivity
questions.correct_answer: Difference in density between the two immiscible liquids
questions.explanation: Immiscible liquids of different densities form distinct layers in a separating funnel, with the denser layer settling at the bottom for controlled drainage via the tap.

questions.question: Why must the stopcock and stem of a separating funnel be pointed away from people, and the tap opened carefully, when shaking a mixture during extraction?
options: To safely release built-up pressure from volatile solvents or gases without spraying liquid at anyone
To make the extraction go faster
To mix the two layers permanently
It has no safety significance
questions.correct_answer: To safely release built-up pressure from volatile solvents or gases without spraying liquid at anyone
questions.explanation: Shaking volatile immiscible solvents builds internal pressure; venting the tap periodically, pointed safely away, prevents forceful, hazardous release of vapour and liquid.

questions.question: What does the term 'molarity' of a solution represent?
options: Number of moles of solute per litre of solution
Number of grams of solute per litre of solvent
Number of moles of solute per kilogram of solvent
Percentage of solute by mass
questions.correct_answer: Number of moles of solute per litre of solution
questions.explanation: Molarity (mol/L or M) is defined as moles of solute divided by the total volume of solution, not solvent alone.

questions.question: How many grams of anhydrous Na2CO3 (molar mass 106 g/mol) are required to prepare 500 mL of a 0.2 M solution?
questions.explanation: Moles required = 0.2 M x 0.5 L = 0.1 mol; mass = 0.1 mol x 106 g/mol = 10.6 g.

questions.question: A standard solution is best described as one whose:
options: Exact concentration is precisely known
Colour is always clear
pH is always neutral
Concentration changes daily
questions.correct_answer: Exact concentration is precisely known
questions.explanation: A standard solution has an accurately known concentration, used as a reference in volumetric analysis such as titrations.

questions.question: A primary standard substance used to prepare a standard solution directly by weighing must have which property?
options: High purity, stability in air, and a known, constant composition
High volatility at room temperature
Strong colour for easy visibility
Hygroscopic nature so it absorbs water readily
questions.correct_answer: High purity, stability in air, and a known, constant composition
questions.explanation: Primary standards (e.g. anhydrous sodium carbonate, potassium hydrogen phthalate) must be pure, stable, non-hygroscopic, and of known formula so an accurate solution can be made by direct weighing.

questions.question: What is the correct first action if concentrated sulphuric acid is accidentally splashed onto the skin?
options: Immediately flush the affected area with copious amounts of running water
Apply a dry cloth and rub the area vigorously
Apply concentrated sodium hydroxide directly to neutralize it
Wait for it to dry before treating
questions.correct_answer: Immediately flush the affected area with copious amounts of running water
questions.explanation: Prolonged flushing with water dilutes and removes the acid quickly, minimizing tissue damage; strong bases should never be applied directly as neutralization generates heat and worsens injury.

questions.question: When diluting concentrated sulphuric acid with water, the correct safety procedure is to:
options: Always add acid slowly to water, never water to acid
Always add water slowly to acid
Mix them together quickly in any order
Heat both before mixing
questions.correct_answer: Always add acid slowly to water, never water to acid
questions.explanation: Adding acid to water allows the large volume of water to absorb and dissipate the heat of dilution; adding water to concentrated acid can cause localized boiling and dangerous spattering.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a fume hood (fume cupboard) in a chemistry laboratory?
options: To remove and vent toxic, corrosive, or flammable vapours away from the technician
To speed up chemical reactions
To store finished experiments
To provide extra lighting for reading burette scales
questions.correct_answer: To remove and vent toxic, corrosive, or flammable vapours away from the technician
questions.explanation: A fume hood draws air through an enclosure and exhausts it outside the building, protecting laboratory personnel from inhaling hazardous fumes during procedures.

questions.question: A Material Safety Data Sheet (MSDS) for a laboratory chemical primarily provides information on:
options: Hazards, safe handling, storage, and emergency measures for the chemical
The market price of the chemical
The chemical's molecular structure diagram only
The supplier's marketing history
questions.correct_answer: Hazards, safe handling, storage, and emergency measures for the chemical
questions.explanation: An MSDS/SDS documents physical and health hazards, handling and storage precautions, and first-aid/emergency response information for a given chemical.

questions.question: Which piece of Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) is essential when pipetting by mouth is prohibited, and instead should always be used?
options: A pipette filler (pump)
A rubber glove on one hand only
A face mask for dust only
An apron made of paper
questions.correct_answer: A pipette filler (pump)
questions.explanation: Mouth pipetting is prohibited in modern laboratories due to the risk of ingesting hazardous chemicals; a mechanical pipette filler/bulb is used instead.

questions.question: What does 'w/v %' (weight/volume percent) concentration mean when a label reads '10% w/v NaCl solution'?
options: 10 g of NaCl dissolved and made up to 100 mL of solution
10 mL of NaCl dissolved in 100 g of water
10 g of NaCl per 10 mL of water
10% of the NaCl molecules are ionized
questions.correct_answer: 10 g of NaCl dissolved and made up to 100 mL of solution
questions.explanation: Weight/volume percent expresses grams of solute per 100 mL of total solution, so 10% w/v means 10 g of solute per 100 mL final solution volume.

questions.question: Before pipetting a corrosive liquid such as concentrated acid, the standard safe practice is to:
options: Use a pipette filler/bulb and work inside a fume hood if the liquid is volatile or fuming
Suck the liquid up gently by mouth using a rubber tube
Pour the liquid directly by hand without a pipette
Use any dry pipette without checking for cracks
questions.correct_answer: Use a pipette filler/bulb and work inside a fume hood if the liquid is volatile or fuming
questions.explanation: Corrosive and volatile liquids must never be mouth-pipetted; a pipette filler and fume hood use protect the technician from exposure and inhalation.

questions.question: In a redox titration between potassium permanganate (KMnO4) and iron(II) solution acidified with dilute sulphuric acid, how is the endpoint detected without an added indicator?
options: KMnO4 itself acts as a self-indicator, giving a persistent faint pink colour at the endpoint
The solution turns completely colourless permanently before the endpoint
A precipitate forms exactly at the endpoint
The temperature drops sharply at the endpoint
questions.correct_answer: KMnO4 itself acts as a self-indicator, giving a persistent faint pink colour at the endpoint
questions.explanation: KMnO4 is intensely purple/pink; once all Fe2+ is oxidized, the next drop of KMnO4 is no longer reduced and imparts a persistent faint pink colour marking the endpoint.

questions.question: Why should dilute HCl NOT be used to acidify a potassium permanganate/iron(II) redox titration?
options: Chloride ions can be oxidized by KMnO4, introducing a side reaction and error
HCl reacts explosively with iron(II) solution
HCl has no acidic properties
HCl changes the colour of KMnO4 to blue
questions.correct_answer: Chloride ions can be oxidized by KMnO4, introducing a side reaction and error
questions.explanation: Dilute sulphuric acid is preferred because sulphate is not oxidized by KMnO4, whereas chloride ions can be oxidized to chlorine, causing an inaccurate titre.

questions.question: What is the correct way to dispose of small quantities of dilute acid or base waste from a routine titration in a standard teaching lab, unless local regulations state otherwise?
options: Neutralize to approximately pH 7 and dispose of via an appropriately labelled sink with running water, following institutional waste policy
Pour directly down the sink undiluted regardless of concentration
Store indefinitely in an open beaker on the bench
Mix all acid and base waste from every experiment into one unlabelled container
questions.correct_answer: Neutralize to approximately pH 7 and dispose of via an appropriately labelled sink with running water, following institutional waste policy
questions.explanation: Standard practice is to neutralize dilute acid/base waste before disposal and to always follow the institution's specific chemical waste management procedures.
